basics.name: Ufuk Cetiner
basics.label: Aeronautical Engineering Student
basics.summary: I’m an Aeronautical Engineering student at Imperial College London with a passion for hands-on design and creative problem-solving. Whether it’s designing systems that fly, float, or fold, I enjoy turning ideas into functional prototypes.

projects.name: Small Scale Wind Turbine Blade Design
projects.summary: Designed, analyzed, and manufactured small-scale wind turbine blades by integrating aerodynamic theory with structural optimization. The project involved iterative testing, simulation, and hands-on prototyping.

projects.name: Formula Student Dashboard & Electronics Enclosure Design
projects.summary: Designed and prototyped multiple solutions working with other systems. Used manufacturing methods such as waterjet cutting and CNC routing.

projects.name: Underwater Robotics MATE Competiton
projects.summary: Lead a team of six students in designing a remotely operated underwater vehicle (ROV) capable of advanced tasks set by the MATE compatiton. Oversaw full project lifecycle: chasis, arm, electronics design; hydrodynamic simulations and underwater testing.

projects.name: On-Demand 3D Printing Serice (GeometricFusion)
projects.summary: Founded an on-demand 3D printing servive based in Istanbul. Lead the operation for a year and had over 50+ completed sales.

projects.name: Underwater Robotics TEKNOFEST Competiton
projects.summary: Lead a team of 12 students in designing a underwater vehicle capable of basic movement and manipulation tasks. Oversaw the full project cycle.

projects.name: Low Cost PET Bottle Recycler
projects.summary: Led a student initiative to design and prototype a low-cost device that transforms recycled PET bottles into 3D printer filament.

publications.name: How a Rotating Orbital Tether Advances Space Travel
publications.publisher: International Journal of High School Research
publications.summary: Explored how momentum-exchanging orbital tethers (Skyhooks) could revolutionize access to low-Earth orbit by reducing propellant needs. Compared the design and economics of such systems to conventional rocket launches, and proposed mechanisms for docking and re-boosting.
